title: Horizon Distance: How Far Can You See?
description: Calculate your horizon distance from any height with Horizon Distance — geometric and refraction-adjusted, for eyes, towers and airliners. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, from a cruising airliner at 35,000 feet the geometric horizon lies about 369 km (229 miles) away — and the horizon itself dips some 3.3 degrees below horizontal.
quick_answer: Horizon Distance estimates how far you can see to the horizon from a given height above the surface. Enter your height — eye level, a cliff, a tower, a summit — and read the distance to the horizon, with the standard-refraction figure beside it.

faq: What is the dip of the horizon?

The angle below horizontal at which the horizon appears: about 0.043° (2.6 arcminutes) at eye level, growing to roughly 3.3° at airliner altitude. Surveyors and navigators correct for it — at sea level it is small, from a cockpit it is not.
Why two numbers — geometric and refraction?

Air bends light gently Earthward, extending the view (modelled as an Earth about 7⁄6 larger). The geometric figure is the guarantee; the refraction figure is the typical day. Exceptional days break both, upward.
Does eyesight or a telescope extend it?
No — optics sharpen what arrives; the horizon is set by geometry and your height alone. Only climbing extends it.
Binocular ships appear 'over' the horizon sometimes?

Refraction again: temperature layers can duct and lift images (superior mirage), letting light from below the geometric horizon reach you. The calculator's standard model is the average; the atmosphere freelances.
Identical — the Great Lakes' long sight lines are pure height-and-distance geometry over very flat water.
Same formula, smaller radius (1,737 km): standing eye height gives about 2.4 km. Astronauts' horizons feel close for a reason.
√(2Rh + h²) is exact for a sphere; the famous √(2Rh) shortcut differs by less than a metre until heights approach a kilometre. This page uses the full form.
The visible sunrise comes early by roughly the dip's worth of Earth's rotation — about 2–3 extra minutes of daylight for a mountaintop observer versus the valley, horizon geometry again.
